title: Introduce opportunistic minimal-span shim and async tail-enrichment pipeline
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Problem: Hot-path span allocation and rich payload encoding are a dominant CPU and memory cost in the inference path, especially for short-lived high-QPS endpoints. Current sampling reduces volume but still forces expensive span marshaling for a subset of requests and retains full trace context.

Goal: Implement a two-stage approach: a minimal-span shim in the request hotpath that captures only essential routing+latency metadata and a lightweight tail-enrichment pipeline that can reconstruct or attach full diagnostic spans asynchronously for sampled tails. This reduces hotpath allocations and encoding while preserving detailed traceability for latency and error investigations.

Design highlights:
- Minimal-span shim: allocate a tiny, fixed-size span object (<128 bytes) with prefiltered fields (route id, tenant id, start timestamp, sampled-tail-token). Avoids tags, logs, and heavy context fields.
- Tail token: short, opaque token embedded in response headers and trace context that allows the enrichment pipeline to rehydrate a richer span later without blocking the request path.
- Async tail-enricher: background service that subscribes to a compact event stream (prefiltered hints or rehydration requests) and performs heavyweight operations (decode request body snapshots, sample heuristics, attach exemplars).
- Admission controller: occupancy-aware adaptive policy that decides which tails are eligible for enrichment based on recent P99 latency, error rates, tenant budgets, and enrichment capacity.
- Fallbacks: preserved compatibility with current sampling; if enrichment fails, minimal-span still provides observability for aggregations.

Why different: existing work focused on deferred encoding and prefilters on the server; this ticket combines a micro-span approach + explicit tail token protocol and a centralized async rehydration service with tenant-aware admission control to limit operational cost while retaining investigability.
acceptance_criteria: Hotpath allocations for span creation reduced by >=40% on p99-qps workload in local benchmarks
End-to-end request latency regression < 0.5% (median) when shim enabled
Enrichment pipeline can rehydrate at least 95% of sampled tail cases under typical load in staging
Response header contains tail token for requests eligible for enrichment
Rollout feature flag allows per-route opt-in and tenant configuration
Integration tests cover shim behavior, tail-token validity, and enrichment failure handling

risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Token leakage or replay could expose sensitive routing metadata. Mitigation: tokens are short-lived, HMAC-signed, and scoped to tenant; ACL checks in enricher service
Risk: Enricher overload causes long queues. Mitigation: admission controller rejects or samples lower when queue depth > threshold and emits stress metrics

Risk: Developers rely on enrichment data being immediate. Mitigation: document expected enrichment latency and surface to console; allow per-route immediate-enrich opt-in for low-throughput debug routes
qa_plan: Load test shim-enabled proxy under synthetic p99 workload and compare heap/alloc profiles
Simulate enricher slowdowns and verify system behavior and metrics
Validate token expiry and ACL paths with integration tests
Canary rollout to 10% of traffic for internal tenants, monitor error percentiles and enrichment success rate
notes: Prefer fixed-size minimal-span struct to avoid heap fragmentation (use stack allocation where possible)
Keep token format compact (<= 32 bytes) to avoid header blowup; explore binary header encoding for gRPC paths
Coordinate with console team for per-tenant knobs and visibility panel
